bib.title: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models

question: What types of legal reasoning can LLMs perform, and how can they be measured in a way lawyers and ML researchers both understand?
contributions: A typology organizing legal tasks by the reasoning type they require (issue-spotting, rule-recall, rule-application, rule-conclusion, interpretation, rhetorical-understanding), drawn from IRAC and related frameworks.
An overview of the 162 tasks, with construction process, dimensions of variation and limitations; full per-task descriptions in the appendix.
An evaluation of 20 LLMs from 11 families, with illustrative studies of model comparison and prompt engineering.

method.summary: 162 few-shot legal tasks (36 corpora) were built by legal-professional co-authors from restructured public datasets and new hand-crafted data, each with a base prompt and 0-9 train demonstrations. 20 commercial and open models were prompted with fixed per-task prompts at temperature 0 and scored with balanced accuracy, F1 or manual grading against an answer guide.
method.task: few-shot legal reasoning benchmark (classification, multiple-choice, extraction, open generation)

datasets.name: LegalBench (162 tasks)
datasets.size: average 563 samples per task, min 50; 28 tasks 50-100, 97 tasks 100-500, 29 tasks 500-2000, 8 tasks 2000+ (Table 12)
datasets.split: train split of 2-8 instances per task (few-shot demos), remainder test
datasets.source: 36 corpora: existing datasets (CUAD, ContractNLI, MAUD, OPP-115, Learned Hands etc.), unreleased scholar-coded datasets, and tasks written for LegalBench; per-task licences in Table 8 (CC BY 4.0 for most)
datasets.preprocessing: existing datasets restructured to binary/multi-class prompts, e.g. CUAD turned into one binary clause-type task per category

models.name: GPT-4
models.params: not stated (believed hundreds of billions for the commercial models)

other.prompt: example tags and explicit output-space instruction added

inference.max_tokens: classification/extraction stopped at newline; rule_qa and rule-application tasks 150 tokens, diversity_jurisdiction_6 300 tokens
inference.samples: 1 run per prompt per item; prompt-sensitivity study uses 5 random demo sets; no repeated sampling or seeds stated for main sweep
inference.prompting: manually written task instructions plus 0-8 in-context demonstrations from the train split (Table 58 lists 0 to 9 per task); same prompts for all models except Claude (added example tags and output-space instruction); rule-application prompts add an instruction to explain reasoning

parameters.demonstrations_per_task: 0 (Canada Tax Court, Consumer Contracts QA, Corporate Lobbying, Intl Citizenship, Rule QA, Supply Chain, SARA numeric) to 9 (Unfair ToS); see Table 58
parameters.prompt_study_demos: 4 demos (2 per class), 5 random draws, 8 binary tasks
parameters.bootstrap: 1000 resamples for error bars; permutation test 1000 resamples

other.hardware: inference for open models on two-GPU GCP 40GB A100 using Manifest library

metrics.name: balanced accuracy
metrics.definition: exact-match, class-balanced accuracy, for classification tasks

metrics.name: F1
metrics.definition: for tasks with multiple classes or extracted terms per instance (successor_liability, ssla_individual_defendants, securities extraction)

metrics.name: rule-application correctness
metrics.definition: proportion of generations that do not misstate fact pattern, outcome or rule, or contain logical/arithmetic error; manual, law-trained grader with answer guide

metrics.name: rule-application analysis
metrics.definition: proportion of generations containing the inferences needed to reach the conclusion; incorrect explanations count as insufficient

metrics.name: sara_numeric accuracy
metrics.definition: prediction correct if within 10% of true tax amount

baselines: GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 vs Claude-1 comparison; 17 open models at 3B/7B/13B
eval.protocol: Paired t-test over tasks within a category for model comparisons; manual grading of rule-application (all samples except 30 per diversity task) and rule_qa by a single law-trained individual; no inter-grader agreement reported; Table 2 averages over tasks in category (rule-application only for 3 models).

availability.data: https://github.com/HazyResearch/legalbench/ (prompts, answer guides and grading guide also released; licences per task)

prompts.text: Does the post discuss public benefits and social services that people can get from the government, like for food, disability, old age, housing, medical help, unemployment, child care, or other social needs? Post: ... Answer: Yes
Reply with either: generic, descriptive, suggestive, arbitrary, fanciful
Diversity jurisdiction exists when there is (1) complete diversity between plaintiffs and defendants, and (2) the amount-in-controversy (AiC) is greater than $75k.

limits: No long-document tasks (context windows were short when the project began).
Only tasks with objectively correct answers; no ambiguity or 'reasonable minds may differ' tasks.
English only, skewed to US law and to contracts and civil procedure; 16 of 17 issue-spotting tasks come from Learned Hands, so issue averages reflect that source.
IRAC steps are evaluated independently, not as multi-hop chains; no analogical reasoning from case law.
Commercial models may have seen tasks in pretraining (Appendix D.2 lists availability: 9 previously published, several original-but-online families, 18 original and unreleased).
No models above 13B open-source; no legal-specific LLMs; prompts not tuned, so scores are a lower bound.
Rule-application and rule_qa graded manually by one law-trained person; no agreement statistic.
Slice analyses are small (n=12-29) and not for rigorous statistics.
Results date from mid-2023; GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Claude-1 are superseded and API versions are not frozen.

Many hand-built tasks have 50-100 items (proa 100, ucc_v_common_law 100, telemarketing_sales_rule 50, rule_qa 50, legal_reasoning_causality 55 test: 31 Yes, 24 No, Table 39), so per-task scores carry wide sampling error; the paper's bootstrap error bars address this only at category level.
personal_jurisdiction is built from 5 base fact patterns in 4 slices, covers only jurisdiction over individuals, and excludes Hertz-style citizenship tests and stream-of-commerce (App F.21).

oral_argument_question_purpose is not a random sample: rarer question types (humor, communicate) were deliberately over-included and common ones (clarification) omitted; questions are from the 2022-23 Supreme Court term only (App F.19).

nys_judicial_ethics questions were reformulated from committee digests by ChatGPT; 2010 and 2021 items are kept to probe leakage, 2022 and 2023 are assumed unseen, but the paper reports no leakage result for this split in App F.17.
SSLA extraction tasks use unformatted PyPDF2 text of at most 2,000 characters; some excerpts omit the named entities, and answers require the official entity name (App F.28).

SCALR covers only single-question Supreme Court cases from the 2001 Term on, keeps the longest 'holding that' parenthetical, and takes distractors by TF-IDF similarity, so difficulty depends on that choice (App F.27).
Supply-chain disclosure labels come from about 400 of about 500 firms, coded by research assistants for summer 2015, so they predate later disclosure practice (App F.30).
ucc_v_common_law excludes mixed-purpose contracts, and telemarketing_sales_rule keeps only clear violations or non-violations and skips 16 C.F.R. 310.3(a)(2)(vi) and (viii) (App F.31, F.33).
opp115 tasks drop snippets under 10 words and the 'other' category; the task text itself calls the task 'simple' for a lawyer (App F.18).
The per-model tables (65-79) give single numbers with no error bars or seeds, and Vicuna columns hit exact 0.0 on many tasks without an explanation in the text.
